words: And your date of birth is?

words: I have your phone number.

words: Yes. Oh, you do? Yeah, you do. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you come directly to Elk River?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: From Lancaster? No, well, I was born there and my folks lived in, I've got to stop and think. Farmington is where Dad went, then he went to school in Coleman for a little while. Now, what did you want, myself, huh? Yeah. You mean when I got married?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When did you first come to Idaho?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: When did we first come to, in 1930.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were you married then? Yes. Why don't you start back and tell me from the time you were born,

speaker: Speaker 2
words: just where you moved and... Okay, okay. Then my folks moved to Farmington, I went to school there, went to La Crosse, and went to school there. And then I went to Lancaster, Washington, where my dad was mail carrier, and Mom got the mail from the people up to the post office. My dad took a stop in the route then. And I took care of the kids, because there was eight of us. And I got married...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were you the oldest?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I was the oldest. I had to take care of the kids. And we lived there a long time. When I turned 17, we got married at Colfax. And then we moved from Lancaster to Deer Park,

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Washington.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Was there, I don't know, three or four months, John was making posts in the Doppler Tether. We just had that little girl, she was about two and a half. Then we left Deer Park, was going to get a job, and we went to Brook, Idaho. And John was going to go into mines. This was cute. I sat out in the car, and he was going around, and he had to have $13 for a house rent, and he had to have, I don't know how much money for a hat, and a flashlight and what have, and it cost more money. We had $2 to our name. So he says, well, I've got to get this job. I said, you can't get a job on Earth without going inside the Earth. There's just no sense of living. He just said, get in the car, get in the car. We cleaned parts, full tan. He went in to see about a job in this place. And we got a job at Neva Hill. The woman was cooking for three men, which would be my husband and two other people. This was in 1930. So we came to Neva Hill, and I did all that for about eight or nine months. I don't know how long it was. I don't know. Our little girl was about three when we came to Elk River then. John got a job here. I was only 22 years old when we came here. And John was working for the Potlatch. It was a hard time. Came on. And I worked for quite a few years at Potlatch. And during the Depression, you know, when June was born, and he was off and on with Potlatch. But you know how it was. There wasn't a job. If there were jobs, the men had work, and otherwise there just wasn't anything. Half the time there wasn't a job, of course. But as a rule, there's always a will, there's a way. And then times got a little bit better. Then later on, while he went to work for Diamond Match, and he worked several years for that. Him and I, we wanted to tear the old back porch off. And from scratch, we started, we built it all by ourselves.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Twelve or twenty-four.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We built a nice bedroom and a dining room. And in the meantime, I was canning. We did all that canning, going to Elk and into canning. We did it all by ourselves. He was taking care of his garden. And so when we got that done, we just barely got it built when the camp shut down. And that was, you know, I'm very bad when it comes to years. But that's, I think that must have been in late 50s?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think, something like that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And as time went on, John worked, then John got maintenance down in, for the city for about five or six years. Till he got a stroke and he had to quit.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But he was past retirement age, wasn't he?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, he was. When he quit, well, let's see. Yes, he was. Well, he was in his 70s, in his 70s when he quit then. Then I got a job out here at the fire patrol. I worked out there about four years.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What kind of work did you do?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I worked in the kitchen with the girls. I guess you'd call me, I don't know. I just took care of the, like, if the girls at the stove were making breakfast, I was helping. And peel potatoes and get vegetables and things. And I would read the salad gal who I was. And did all that. If they needed help for a lot of different things, I just helped them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you had your dinner where it needed.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Wherever I was needed. But my transportation was so bad, later on I couldn't work there because I had no way of going in and no way of coming up. It was funny, I went out there. Well, I think we had breakfast early. I went out there early in the morning. Then we'd come in about seven or eight. And then we had to go back for dinner, then come back after dinner, and then go back in for supper, and come back after supper. So there were six trips that I had to fight for, and half the time I didn't have no way of going. And part of the time I walked. And that's a long way to walk, and you get up so early. And then at that time, they didn't have things so convenient like they have now. And you had lots of fires, and you can kind of get up at two o'clock and go. Oh, two, three hundred sandwiches. And, but I loved making sandwiches.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: This was big for the firefighters?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: This was for the firefighters. And they got a whole bunch of guys from all over. And I'm going to forget the time we made, oh, a lovely one, lunch and stuff. They took it in a helicopter, or a plane. They took it in a plane, and when they dropped it down, it went in the river and lost everything. All that goody, goody, goody stuff. And that's really something to think about. I wish now I had made a diary from the time I started to work, because there was a lot of things went on that I, that I could have said, but I imagine I've forgotten. But I worked with two nice gals. One has passed away now, but I think the other one would go back again this summer. Who she's going to get the help, I don't know. But I could have worked there longer if I had transportation.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When you don't have a car,

speaker: Speaker 2
words: it always told me to go get a bicycle, but I told them that was out of the question to me, because I've never driven, I never rode a bicycle in my life. I wasn't about to start.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You weren't going to start now. No. Would you drive if you had a car?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I presume, I used to drive all the time, but my husband got a stroke,

speaker: Speaker 1
words: and we had to get rid of our car,

speaker: Speaker 2
words: because I couldn't trust him with it, he couldn't trust himself. And I always said, gee, it's too bad that we didn't keep our car, and you had your health, then I would have transportation. Yes, I think if we'd have had a car, I think I would have taken up driving. Because that's a little way back, but we just didn't have one, so. But that's all over the, that's all in the past now. I really did enjoy working out there with the girls. It was early in the morning and late at night, but it was something I could look forward to. I come home at 8 o'clock in the morning, and I'd be through out there for the morning, and come in and do my work in here, and half the time, Tom would still be sleeping. You know, a lot of people don't get up until, well, maybe they would be getting up at 8 o'clock in the morning, and I'd have a third of my work done. So it was nice. I really thoroughly enjoyed it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What time would you get up to go out there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I had to get up, it all depends, most of the time I'd get up at 5. Sometimes I'd get up at 4, because I had to be out there. Well, they had different shifts that they had to get going in. Sometimes it was firefighters and stuff, and there seemed to be an awful lot of fires for some reason when I was working. And now they've got everything much more handy in the kitchen. They've got steam tables and different things, where at that time we didn't have much of anything to work with.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You had to cook it right there and get it to their table.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, we'd have these fireboys, we'd hear a fire school, and there'd be hundreds of boys, and there'd be at least five deep and long string of them, and it was cold and rainy, and they couldn't eat in the kitchen, they had to go outside and eat, or in their cabins or stuff, because there's too many of them. But I enjoyed it. I got to see a lot of different faces.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They come from all over?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: All over.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: To learn how to fight fires?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh-huh, and they show them how to fight fires and stuff. And I don't know if they've done that lately or not, but they used to have last year, but they've still been going on like they used to have.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long ago was this when you quit?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: When I quit? Oh, I was just trying to think. That's in the late 60s, I think.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So maybe five years?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, oh yes, all of that, maybe six years. I guess I got all my record down there, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So they must have really ate big meals.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, they are. Yeah, we fed them good, yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They had to have a lot of power.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, at that time, they had like a, better than a store. But I don't think they do it now anymore. They don't cook like they used to, but we had a big, even a butcher shop. They had a certain man there who did all the butchering, I mean, taking care of the meat. And they had a big cellar that had all the, anything you wanted, there was nothing that you didn't want, you couldn't have, to cook with. So it's fun cooking when you've got your stuff to cook with. Yes. And I really enjoyed it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And they started from scratch then on everything, the freshly killed.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, well, I don't know, they did so much, no, they'd get it in. But we'd have fresh chicken and stuff, and he'd always get a half a beef or something like that, or half a pig or something, and he'd cut it up.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Imagine they use a lot of frozen stuff now.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, now I presume that, oh yeah. Because they don't get, they don't have that filling out there no more, and cutting up, and then they used to have food cooked and stuff. But it's just different. I haven't been out there, they've asked me to come out there, but one of these days maybe I will walk out.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It might be interesting to see how it is.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, to see what's going on. See all the new stuff that we got. So maybe I will one of these days go out there, and it'd be kind of interesting.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, I would think so. Well, let's go back to this now. I'm lost. Now, where did you first come when you came to Idaho?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: When I first came to Idaho, we came to Neva Hill, which is Neva Hill no more.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's up near Spokane.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no, that's right out here. Between Elk River, right on Elk River, between Elk River and Bouleville. About, oh, I didn't see. Twelve, thirteen miles out. Used to have a schoolhouse there and a depot, but there's nothing there now. And we came in here in 1930 into Elk River.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, and that was, let's see, what year?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You came to Elk River. When you went to Neva Hill.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, that was, well, let me see. We went to Neva Hill in 1930 in May, and then we came into Elk River, I guess that fall.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How did you travel? Did you have a car?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, we had an old Maxwell car. The cutest thing was when we was coming into Neva Hill to get this job from Spokane, we had this Maxwell and we had a little trunk in the back. So my husband got out, we got lost, and he stopped the car and he got out and took all the bedding out and put it under a tree. And he says, okay, you and the baby come out now, I've got the bed all made. And I says, I'm not going to go out there in that bed with my baby, the bears will get us. He said, oh, come on, you're so tired. And I says, no, I wouldn't get out of that car for love nor myself. So he went, he just left again, rolled the doll up, stuck it in the car. And when I woke up, I was really tired. I had a husband on one shoulder and a baby in my arms and me all cramped. But we made it okay. Got into Elk River, but we were lost. And that was out by Deary, the other side of Deary. When we used to go up the hill, we had to go this way. But we come here, John got a job here. And we've been here ever since.

speaker: Speaker 2

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So this was... actually, was your father's appointment as postmaster or...

speaker: Speaker 2

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So that portion of it, she took it, got it from the depot to the post office.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: From the post office to the... She had a little wagon thing that she used to take. It wasn't too far away.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How old were you when you were left to take care of these eight kids?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh dear, I was... I must have been 10, 11 years old.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So she just left the house.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: At that time, I could do more things now than the girls could at 16 and 17, because I had the responsibility. I even had to cook while she told me what to do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long would she be gone?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, not very long. Oh, half hour to hour, 45 minutes. She wouldn't be gone too long.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But you pitched in and did things while she was gone.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, and the kids were pretty good. They were pretty good kids, you know, for... That was only once a day that she was gone like that. But she never left us very much. I did a lot of work. Well, I did the boys' work, because my dad... I have two brothers, but I'm the oldest. And my dad was a mail carrier, and he had to have hay for his horses. So every... So often in the summertime, I'd have to go out and help him rake the hay, cut the hay, rake the hay, put it on the rack and bring it in, put it in the barn, because he had to have feed for the horses. And for some reason or another, I was the only one that was available to help him, because the boys were too small. And I'd come in and help Mom, you know. So we... I just had... I did... Well, we went to bed early, too, and got up early, and we just didn't have the things like we did now. I just was raised a different... Oh, many times I'd be out there. I'd be out there raking and stacking hay, shocking hay, and the Fourth of July, and I didn't get to do the things like we used to get to do now. And the kids would go by and say, oh, come on in, let's go to St. John, there's a big doings there. Well, I couldn't go because I had to help my folks. So for a long time, I kind of held that against my folks. But now I understand. They had to have me to help them. I suppose Dad could have got someone else, but the money question and such.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, it would have been money out.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, and so... And he knew that I could do it, or he'd teach me how to do it. And so that was one of the things that I did that... Nowadays, the kids don't do that, especially girls. But it didn't hurt me, you know. Well, I can't say it helped better than any, but I knew what was going on now than before I did it. When I did work, I thought they... I can't say they were cruel to me, but I just thought that I shouldn't have done it. But now I can understand why they... The money-wise and stuff. When you're young, why you just kind of resent it, I guess.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, you must have wanted to go.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I did want to go so bad with the boys and girls. I was a school kid. Oh, I was 13, 14 years old, and I couldn't... I was a big girl, too. I didn't get to do any of that stuff. It was foolish to... My dad was so old-fashioned that it was foolish for you... If you had work at home to do, you do your work, and if you don't have time to go anywhere, you just don't have the time, you do your work. And if it's too late, you just don't go. So that's where now...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's the way it was.

speaker: Speaker 2
