speaker: Speaker 2
words: She had a doctor? We had doctors.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Doctors came in the house. Uh-huh. Does Marilyn have an occupation? Yes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She's... In Torrey, Idaho, she's a... What would you call it? Postman. She works in the post office. Every Saturday she works at the post office. And then any other time when one of them doesn't... When one of them leaves or something, then she fills in. Sometimes she works for a week at a time, and then the other time she just works Saturday. And on Saturdays she locks the post office at 7.30. So I'm kind of proud of her. I think that she... took that civil service job...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: She took the exam.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Examination. She said there's 40 of them, and she happened to be the one that got the job. A real pleasing crowd.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Good for her. Yeah. Uh-huh. Did you go to high school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I went to the eighth grade. No. Just the eighth grade.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you ever hold a job? Before you were married.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I worked in a store once in a while, yeah. For about four or five months only.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Clerking?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh-huh. In a store.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And since then, since lately you've been a cook.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes. Take care of my husband.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You make... you crochet?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I crochet all the time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And I think your daughter told me you make a lot of clothes. Sewing. Sewing.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I love to do... And quilt! I've got a quilt. I don't know what you call it, but I'm just crazy about making quilts. I made this one. I went to Spokane and made two there for our genie, and then I've made... I bet you I've made seven quilts in the last six months. Now I've got one started for our younger daughter.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Are these pieced quilts?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh-huh. I got... I'll have to show them to you after a while. I got them put together. Yeah, I really enjoy it. And then I'm making flowers out of beads.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, you made all these?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I just... I wish I lived somewhere where I could just go and get the stuff and just... because I love to make pretty things.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But you do need a supply.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah, that's right. You can't buy it down here, and Mosca doesn't have too much of a variety.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Aren't there some mail-order houses?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know. Maybe there is, but you know, when you want to make something, I just like to go to town, pick it up, and come home and make it. We're in Spokane. We just went to town, and I bought all that stuff, and genie did too. We came home and got it all together, and it's fun to make pretty things. In the Easter time, we got some different things, and we made little Easter rabbits out of... Oh, just everything we could find. I made little baskets for... put feathers in it. So it's kind of fun to make stuff like that. But I really enjoy making beads. I'm not too good with it, but I'd like to learn more about it. And Christmas time, I made Mr. and Mrs. Santa Claus from... soap containers, you know. I made all these clothes that just darling.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: There's all kinds of things like that you could do.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, but it's hard to get anything in the Elk River because there's nothing... They can't carry all that stuff because they don't have the... people wanting the stuff that we need. Mm-hmm. Like if I want something, maybe somebody else doesn't want it. But the bigger stores can have it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, right. There's more people. Are there any other jobs you've held besides cooking in the lumber camp? No. And in the store?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, not a lot.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you talked about your hobbies. I have that down here. Have you ever gotten any awards or ribbons?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. You know, everybody says, if you sold a... what would you charge? And I say, well, I've never made a thing in my life and sold it. Where my husband makes baskets himself. I think it's just because when I make something and there's like a break that comes up or somebody says, oh, that's beautiful, then I just give it to them. Whereas I suppose if I lived out where it's a bigger city, where there'd be more demand and stuff, I could sell stuff.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Maybe when your husband goes to these things like the Renaissance Faire, you should take some of your quilts along.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I suppose. I thought of taking...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Demonstrating how you do it. Then they'd be there to sell them.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But I, yeah, I suppose. But you know what makes it bad? If you had a car of your own where you could just take your stuff and put it in your trunk and... but you have to borrow somebody else and you hate to leave it in their car.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Right. You keep running into that all the time.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh-huh. And there's your throwback for not having a car of your own. Right. So that's why we're trying to... We wish we could sell our house and get where... Well, I wouldn't even mind Troy because you could get out once in a while to Moscow, to Lewiston. And I think we'd be so isolated. And I don't think there'd be so much snow there either. Because my husband is not allowed to do any shoveling. And sure as the world, I don't care nothing about shoveling because I don't have the help like I used to have either.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, it certainly stays on longer here.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, yes. It's been two months ago that it finally left us.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes, well, there was still some piled up around when we were in May.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I think maybe six weeks ago they had snow. Yes. So it... I'm not... I like snow, but I don't like all the snow that I have to shovel, you know. But I do love my home. But it's like I say, there's lots of advantages and disadvantages living in Elk River. For the younger generation, they can have a car, they got their own thing, and they can go when they want to. Where you get older, you can't do the things you'd like to do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Right. You're independent. Right.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Right. And I like to be independent. I just have always have been, and that makes it tough.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Are you a member of a club?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I do that. Yes, I belong to that birthday club. I've belonged for quite a while. And Rebecca, I used to belong to Rebecca. I just now resigned from her, and I wish I had never done it, but I did. The only reason I did, we took our Rebecca lodge out of here and took it to Deary. And as I said before, there's no way of going down unless you bum a ride. And so I just had...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: um... resignation.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I could join any time I wanted to back again, because I'm in good standing. Until we do find a place to live or anything, and I can all reinstate. But I used to... I belonged to lodge for... well, I think since 1948, I think.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's a long time.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's a long time. Yeah, something like that. Forty-eight, I think. And, uh... And just this club here, this birthday club, is the only thing I belong. They used to have a grammar club, but they...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: you know, it's fizzled out. Uh, do you participate in the community church? What? Do you help with the community church, or are you interested in that? Oh...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. Uh, we go to church once in a while, but they never ask us for any, you know... but I would like to help if they needed. Oh, I have helped in the summertime with the children for two weeks in a school. It's a Bible school. I have helped with that, which was nice. But I didn't this year. No, not last year either. It's a problem sometimes to... well, they get different ones, I presume, with the people that work with them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I'm sure there are probably... like other places, they're always hunting for people to help, too. Okay, that takes care of the data, and I got a lot of other stuff at the same time. So, uh, I'll go through these questions, and some of them you've already answered. So maybe you just add to it. You talk about the advantages and disadvantages of living in a rural town. It's hard to get out. Yeah, it really is.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: As I said before, my husband was real sick one night, and you know, you're just all by yourself. Of course, thank God for the phone. But I was just thinking, the person lived close by. You just run, call the doctor up, and he'd either come to your house, or he'd go to the hospital. But so far, thank God, with all prayers and stuff, it seems like there's things that do help you, and there's always a will, there's a way. So far, it's because he was real sick there not too long ago. It seems like he gets these dizzy spells, and the meaning kind of scares me, which I know you don't feel good. But otherwise, why, I do love it here. It's cool and...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It's pleasant.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, and it's not noisy in the smog, you know what I mean. But in other words, in other ways, if we lived in the... Well, my daughter lives, our daughter lives in, um, Fort Canning, in the valley. And, um, we'd love to live there, but we wanted a trailer, they got about three acres to put there, but for some reason, they don't allow nice trailers there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They've made a regulation here.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Evidently, it's agriculture, but... I still wish that David does have a real nice... I'd like to get one of those houses on those trailers, but it's just like a house. And I thought, well, someday maybe I'd just go and talk to those guys, but I never have had the... Well, I guess it takes a lot of guts and stuff to talk to them, and... Because they have their regulations, too. Yes. And I would just like to... They put a, uh, basement, but that had nothing to do with it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But in some way that you could make it...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They say there's a loophole, but if you get around about it, you could maybe do it, but I don't... So far, I haven't found the loophole, you know. I don't know what to do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I understand.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's all I know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you've been spent some time in Spokane.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, every summer we try to go to... just to get away from Elk River for a while, and... Well, it's just nice to get away, but it's nice to come home, too, have some place to come home to. How does...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You've talked a little bit about what life was like when you grew up. There's a lot more hard work. Oh, yeah. Not as much recreation. Did your family do anything for recreation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not... the only thing they ever did for us was get up early in the morning and do all their work. No, no recreation. When I think of the kids now, they've got so many nice things to do, but my folks didn't do anything to make it pleasant for the children. All they thought was work. I presume that's what they grew up with, work, and so they just passed it on. I swore if I had 50 kids, they would do the things I had to do. And I made it... If my girls wanted to go to the dances at 12 years old, I went with them and we had a good time, and they had a good time. But my folks wouldn't let us go to the dances. They wouldn't let us play cards. And with my girls, I'd say, well, if they wanted to have a bunch in and make ice cream, I didn't care. They could have the kitchen and just do... and they made a mess. That's all right. It's home, and they had all their family. When I was a kid at home, they wouldn't let us do that. They just didn't believe in it. You were just made to your honor for the work, and that was it. I had a different viewpoint from my children. And I think my kids grew up... They all three graduated, which I'm so proud of, and so I think we did a real good job raising our children.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Your husband spent time away, too, didn't he? Yes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Camp. Yes. When our last girl was born in Indicot, I brought her... We brought her home at... Lots of snow. Three weeks old, I think. And this house, when we bought... When he bought it, there was nothing. It just was just a shell. And I remember we had a bed out in the front room, and I had... And the other two girls were scared to keep alone because, well, their daddy wasn't home, and this is me with an airtight stove, and it was cold. And I had to sit home with them because we could only move once a week. And when you talk with... It don't last a whole week. I'd have to sit in my little bed,

speaker: Speaker 1
words: take care of a baby,

speaker: Speaker 2
words: and the children, get them off to school. Yeah, I met normal at school then, too. And it was a hard life to do all that stuff and raise your kids. Then you'd get home Saturday night while you'd Sunday afternoon.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That wasn't very long at home.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, it wasn't.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So he had to live out in the woods in the camps.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, he did. And then he'd be home just long enough to fit some wood and get the things he had to have done, and then I'd have to do his laundry and stuff. And he always had a bunch of guys go back with him, you know, in the pickup. So it was hard for both of us.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How many years did this go on?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, up till it closed up. I just don't remember when the camps closed up. It must have been the late 60s.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, quite a while. Thirty years.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes, all of that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, that is a lifetime of working.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, it was.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And that's what most of the men in Elk River did, then. Yeah. So you were mostly women and children here during the week.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's when they had that big fire out here. Just men were all at the fires out here all the time. And the women were just here by themselves. And the children, and just had to... Well, each one had to take care of their... Each family had to take care of their own family and help others if they could, if they possibly could.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How long did you... Was your courtship?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My husband and I? Well, I went with him when I was 13 years old and got married when I was 17.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Four years. Yeah, courtship.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. I was just too young to get married. So it was off and on. I didn't go in constantly, but...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You were in school.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But I was in school and then we had activities. I didn't get to do the things like the girls do now. I get to make scenes. Now, these kids would go to a soda fountain or something like that. But we didn't have a soda fountain. And if I'd just go to some girl's house, and he'd have to be there, or to a store, and he'd have to be there. But I can remember going to church, and I meant to say, yeah, church and show. And my mother would let me go by myself. She'd go with me, which was all right, too. I was only about 14 years old. And outside that, I wasn't much of anything. Of course, she liked the shows, too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: She went to the shows. Your father probably didn't.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, my dad didn't. I don't know anything.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When you...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What was expected?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did they get you through the eighth grade and that sort of thing?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I think more my dad was worried about was me. Staying home and working, you know. He thought that that was enough. Why go to school when you don't need it? You're just going to get married anyway. You don't need that education. They didn't believe in education. Although he went to university in Poland.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Your father did? Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But that's a man, see? Uh-huh. These German people, they just think the men need education because they've got to take care of family. A woman doesn't need the education. She's going to raise a family, and why should she need education?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was that true for your other brothers and sisters?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, there was eight of us, and I think there's four or five of us graduated. I was one that only went to the eighth grade. But none of my brothers graduated. They went to, I think, the eighth and ninth grades themselves. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Your father didn't think it was important then for them to get more education? No?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because, see, my younger brother, I can remember. I don't remember too much about my older brother because he was gone most of the time. But I know my younger brother, at 13, he was driving a hit and a box, and that's four horses or more. And he took a man's job, you know? Of course, at that time, Dad expected us. When Dad expected of us, we expected of us ourselves that we had to do it. And he made so much money. And I can remember I was about 13, and I had to go work for this lady. She had a baby, and I took care of the baby and did all those dishes and separated the milk, washed the separator. I came home, I think it was a dollar and a half a week. My dad took the money. I never get to see the money, you know? And that's the kind of stuff that they believed in. You know, they didn't believe, why should you have any money? You don't need it. You're getting all your food at home. You don't need nothing else. Uh-huh. Well, nowadays, children have to have money to... Well, a lot of them, it's different. They like to have their... I like, myself, I like to have my own money. If I wanted to buy somebody something, I like to say, well, I bought it for you. But my dad thought, well, you don't need the money. You don't have to have it for nothing. You get all your eating, sleep, clothes. What else do you want with it? And so that's the kind of belief that he had. So there is a big difference.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you remember what you had in mind when you were getting married? Was it to escape from home?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You bet I did. You bet I did. Many times I would have loved to run away, and I don't know where I would have run to, but I even told my folks I was going to run away. And they said I better not. I wish now I had the guts like I have today. I would have run away because...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You said you had a cramp in my finger.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I tell you, it slipped away from me every day.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But I swore if I ever got married and had any children, if they said they wanted a dollar for something, I'd want to know what it's for.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I'd get another thing, another one.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: If I know they want a dollar and I want to know what it's for, if it's something that they want, I was going to give it to them. I believe anyone, any individual should have their own say. If you haven't, I'd just say, well, I don't have it now, but maybe tomorrow. But I don't just say, well, you don't need it. Because I don't believe there's such a thing as you don't need it. There is a cause for it. That's my belief.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: There are needs other than physical needs.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I believe that way because...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You know when a person gets along, there's something wrong all the time.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: When what? I didn't get you.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I say when a person gets along, there's something.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Get long?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh!

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, that's what I thought you meant, but you didn't say that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I didn't say, oh. Did I say it wrong? I used to go jump around, run around. I can't get... When I go get a wool, get it in the brush, I get tangled up, fall down. Yeah. Oh, yeah. I get up and go again. Good for you. I don't give up. Good, good. That's good. That's the only way you'll get anyplace, isn't it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, you bet.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was, were you pleased after your marriage? Yes. You just had more freedom then.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, and you know, there's a lot of things that I got after I was married that I never had when I was at home. And I was really happy. John's a lot older than I am, but he took me and he raised me and he, and I'm not a bit before I ever got married, and I really aren't. I'm not a bit, because all those things, we don't agree. I don't agree to some of the things that he does, but maybe just some things that I do that he don't agree with. And I think, well, he lets me do more or less what I want to do, you know, and he knows if I want to do it, that I must know what I'm talking about. Maybe I'm not right sometimes, but maybe I'm not wrong. But, no, I'm not a bit sorry.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But you are an adult and you can make some...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Make my own decisions what I want to, and of course I always wanted to get married and have babies myself. I'm just like Sonia, I wanted a family.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And your babies were pretty well separated. Did it just happen that way?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I was at, because when we had Jean, she was married two years, John was there, she was at home, and he said there would be no more children. So I thought, well, okay, that's fine.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You thought this was kind of a hard thing for a woman to have to do.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, he just, I could still see him. He had big tears streaming down his face. But anyway, after she came and everything was so beautiful, we just loved it. And then we came here and then Norma was born. And I told him, I said, Norma, we were expecting Norma. He just couldn't believe it when we got her. Oh, that was just great. But we didn't, wasn't too happy over poor little Marilyn, but oh, she was a joy. But each one of my, you can put your, it might be nice to have them all together, but they're nice to have them that way too, because each one had their own way of coming into the world, and their own way of, well, each one could take care of the other one like this. She was about 15 years old, was 14 years old, I guess. And we just, and I, when I knew that, I was, oh, I was so, I wasn't embarrassed, but I was so disgusted, let's put it that way, because the other two were in school. And then here she came along, but oh, she's my little blonde girl. She's really something. So I re-enjoyed all three of them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, this is kind of a private question, and you don't have to answer if you don't want to, but how would you have limited your births in those days?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: How would I have limited? You mean I would have had more?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: If you were having more and you really didn't want any more.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I would like to have more. Uh-huh. I would really like to have more.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But like he said, you didn't, he didn't want any more.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He didn't want any more, so he had to control, but evidently it was him that didn't want any more, but I did, I would like, I wanted two girls and two boys. Of course, we got the three girls, but I wanted a family, but I didn't want eight of them like my mother did, because I didn't know whether he could provide, but I think a large family, if there's, there wasn't too much love in our home except amongst our kids. We had lots of love amongst our kids. We didn't fight like most kids do nowadays. If one got in trouble, we never, we never rat on the other one. We, we always, when one was in trouble, we were always on the same side, and which was beautiful.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But now they're kind of held together against the adults.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And we knew that Dad was very strict, and, well, we just, someone say, well, where's Adeline, or where's so-and-so? Oh, she's out here playing. Maybe she'd be at the neighbors, and there she wasn't supposed to be there. So when the other kids, when they'd go get her and bring her back, before anybody could ever know where she was even gone, she was there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They kind of protected each other.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Each one of us took care of one another, so that was beautiful, too. You know, and that's one of the beauty things I can think about my childhood life, was all the sticking together of kids.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When your children were small, what kind of medical facilities did you have in Elk River?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My own kids? Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, we were lucky.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I guess we were, we were lucky here, because our doctors in Dr. Drury and Troy, Dr. Drury wasn't there all the time. That's the only doctor I know that's in Troy.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: There was a time earlier when they had kind of a hospital here, wasn't there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Long ago. Yes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: There was a doctor here, sure, and a hospital up on the hill. But the doctor was up on the hill when Normandine was supposed to be born, I think a week before he left, and she wasn't. So he took off to get a car at Michigan. And there was a doctor in Bouleville, and this Dr. Bouleville came into Elk River. Well, when I knew she was, I was expecting, I went to the neighbors. We had no point, but they had a phone, and they called the doctor in Bouleville, and he came. And, of course, we were new, but they didn't, not very many people knew us, but they knew the people that we called, and they told, gave them their name and everything. So that was the only reason, but the doctor was, I didn't go to the hospital here. I had our baby at home. Yeah, he came here. Yeah, so, and, but it was, it was, it was, I'll tell you about John, this is really cute. He's at camp, and I didn't know whether to call John or call the doctor. But as the time got on, I thought, well, now I've got to make a decision because things is telling me what to do. So I said to Mrs. Simmons, I don't know what to, to call John or, or, or should I call the doctor? She said, I think you'd better call the doctor. So I called the doctor, and they called John, too. Well, at that time, they had big fires out there, too. And this guy that was supposed to bring him in on a speeder was out all night, and he didn't have the guts to ask them to bring him in. So he walked all the way, I think it's 50 to 20 miles, but he ran all the way in, and he came in, and I was so surprised to see him. Well, anyway, he came in the kitchen, and the doctor had some stuff in the sink. He dumped stuff out of his pan, was going to wash his hands, and I guess it was some of the solution that the doctor had put in there. But it was so cute because he was coming in there, and of course he didn't want to do it where we were until he had his hands washed. And the doctor was, you're in here dumping out all my stuff, whatever it was, and I thought that was kind of cute of him. I think he was here by the time he got there. And Marilyn's was born in Hollis, too, at IndyCut. But the doctor was only across the street there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So it was easier to get home.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I went home. IndyCut's only about 13 miles from where my folks live in Lancaster, and Lancaster's just a wide spot in the road. Do you know where Colfax is?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes, I know where Colfax is.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, do you know where Lancaster is?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It must be nearby.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, it's not too far away. Anyway, I had a sister in IndyCut, and I stayed there with them, and there was our doctor there. So a doctor, and they said, well, what are you expecting, a girl or a boy? I said, well, I'll tell you, I'm really expecting a girl. And what's your name? Oh, Marilyn Ann. Well, now what are you going to do with this boy? Are you going to call him Andy? Well, I might call him John Rangel. That was my doctor's name, Rangel. I might call him John Rangel, but it was a little girl, so. She was still Marilyn Ann. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did you do for recreation and relaxation when your girls were growing up?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: When my girls were growing up? Well, I'll tell you. They had lots of parties, I guess, more or less. Like I said, they made their own ice cream, and they brought their boyfriends up, and we had porn. At that time, we didn't have any TV, of course, but they had the pornographic that listened, and the radio, and they'd have dances at the school, and we had dances at places. If they wanted to go, they could go to the dances, and they had places they wanted to go down and have Coke or pop, or they'd go to the girl's friend's house. Now, Norma June was a great girl to go to the neighbor's house and play paper dolls. And where Jeannie and Norma, Jeannie and Marilyn were bookworms. They'd go out, and they'd come home, and they'd go in their room, and they'd read the books. Norma was more or less, she liked to have company. To this day, she loves company. But they played paper dolls. They'd get a big Sears and Roebuck catalog, and cut all these pretty girls out and make their own fun.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What did the... Thank you for learning so much here, Nelson.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, at that time, the women didn't do too much. I think they just took care of the children. And at that time, we had trains coming in here, and the mail would come in along to the girls all with their buggies, with the babies, go down, they had the children, and get the mail, and they'd go to the restaurant, or more or less to the drugstore. We used to have a fountain there. We still do, but this was another bigger fountain.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was this Morris' drugstore? Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And then they had another one that's a cafe. It was real nice, where all the family went in, and we'd take our babies down there and get our mail, and go down and have a Coke, or mostly ice cream. And then the little kids would have ice cream. And it was just like a parade with the, well, when Marilyn was born, I bet there was, no, when Norman was born, they had, oh, goodness sakes, I bet there was 50 or 20 kids born that time. And also when Marilyn was born, they had quite a few children. But it was a hard winter. Lots of youngsters here. But then if you wanted to, you'd go down and get your mail, come home, write a letter, and it would go out around 4 o'clock.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It was a lot better.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It would go out around 4 o'clock.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It was a lot better.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It seemed like it was a different life than it is now. For some reason, I thought it was. I loved it myself because I didn't like it because he was gone all the time, but I knew that was one of the things that we had to live with.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You just put up with it. Yeah. That's what the job required.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because if you want some bread and butter on your table, why not put your head up and camp with it?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And everybody in Elk River worked for Potlatch. Right.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: More than everybody did.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Except for people like the drug dealers.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Like the storekeeper and the butcher.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: People like that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What, you have friends in now, and mostly just visiting and going to fairs and things like that. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, a lot of times we make sauerkraut and stuff, you know, and I make a dish that's called sarmas. It's got meat and rice and a bunch of stuff, and it's rolled up like little cabbage leaves. Well, birthdays mean, we're a very post-knit family, and birthdays mean more to us than a lot of people that does at Christmastime.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So we always have a big meal,

speaker: Speaker 2
words: big dealie at Christmastime, anniversaries, birthdays, and have a house full of people. And if they can't come when the dinner's on the table, if they feel like coming later on and talking to us or just come in for a snack or a cup of coffee, they come in, you know, and that was a big, that there is a big thing in Elk River, you know. Some people, it's more or less not, but it is a big deal with us. And I see Norma June, they'll have an anniversary coming up, and then we're going to do something real great for them too now, and then like Sonja will have one too before long, and that'll be, of course it's always their friend, with their families too, because the families come in, and they have their own family. And now when we have this for Norma now, her big birthday thing, Sonja wants it at her house, which will be tomorrow night. Well, I'm going to make the buns, and now she's going to make the cake for, and I'm going to make ice cream and make some buns and different things, and salad. We all get together and pitch in, and each one of us brings only two or three things, and I might even go to the basement and see if I can beat some stuff or pick up some stuff to help out on the table.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You still do a lot of canning.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I do a lot, if I can get the jar lids, that's the next question. That's the problem. See, I haven't had any jar lids for a couple of years now. Well, last year was my main one, the year before I had a few, but last year I didn't get any to speak of. And someone says you can get it, but you have to order it back east somewhere, but I don't know exactly where to order them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The extension could tell you that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What's that?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You know, the extension service. Do they come out?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know where that is. When they say that, down here at the store, they can get it if you put in your order, but if you put in your order sometimes, and you're not there to get it, somebody else will get it. So what? I've only got one family here that got two cases.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You mean somebody else had ordered it and they were down there when they arrived.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And they got two cases of it or three, whatever it was, and which before when they get stuff in like that, they didn't sell it in cases.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You mean the agriculture extension service doesn't come out to Elk River?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Not that I know of.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They have kind of a homemakers group, and they give help like that and recipes and things like that. Well, you know, I can call there in Moscow, of course that's Latak County, but this is Clearwater County. She might be able to tell me, you know, if there's another organization here.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, we could know what to get. I'd love to get at least four or five dozen because I do like a can. One year I canned, let's see, it was 68 quarts of just carrots out of my garden.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you have a garden now?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, no, Johnny isn't able to go out. We told somebody else to have our garden, but we get some stuff.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They share stuff.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They share it with us. Because he's not able to do anything. He bends down, he gets dizzy, and I just don't want him to get hurt or anything out there. That's no sense when you don't feel good. Now, all this stuff comes up, we'll have a little bit of garden too, from what they've got planted.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So it would be helpful if he'd be able to can this.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I love it. I've still got carrots left from when I get the kids. I was going to say about the sauerkraut. I've still got sauerkraut. We make our sauerkraut and then I can it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It doesn't get quite so sour.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It doesn't get so sour and it don't get so soft. I get a certain stage and I can it. But see, we didn't make any last year because we didn't have no jar lids. So you have to stop and think that. But if I get some jar lids, I am going to get a few things to can. And it really comes in handy.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When the children were growing up, did you ever worry about what would happen if your husband were injured or killed or something? I never.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That bothered you? Yes, yes, I did. And he's been hurt many a time. I wondered if, of course, he goes to the hospital, I just wondered when it would be that he'd get to come home or if he ever did get to come home. Yes, many a time. I relied on my children quite a bit. And I think we kind of stick together too. Especially your oldest one. I don't know why you kind of lean on them. They're just children, but you kind of do lean on them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And what happened in Elk River if a man was killed? What did the widow do?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What would the widow do? Well, I don't know. Not like this girl, she lost her husband. She just, of course, she's young. She came home to her folks. But there's others that lost their husbands and their children are quite big. They just stay here. Well, one of them, another one, her husband just died from a heart attack. But she moved out and will never come back. She just can't stand to come back. I think that's all individuals, however you feel about it. Some can come back and some can't.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did the company have insurance or some kind of monetary support?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I imagine if you're working, well, I don't know too much, but I imagine if you're working for that company, they would have to have some kind of insurance. Of course, we have our own, you know. You've got to have a supplement of something, even if you are on Medicare.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Medicare is not, for me,

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Medicare don't mean nothing to me, you know, because you've got to pay the first 60 anyway. And after that, well, maybe you don't even need it the next year. Then you have another 60 dollars if you need it, you know. So you have to have something to rely on.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Right, right. Was there, there wasn't such a thing as welfare in the old days?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, no, that's what it, no welfare, no food stamps, no nothing that I ever know of.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did the women have to just get housework to do, or what could they do?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Ironing and housework. I did a little ironing. I did a little bit of that, and there's no pay in it, so, but it's enough to keep a little bit of stuff on the table. I took in a little bit of ironing and a little washing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, when he was injured and in the hospital, did his pay was cut off? Yes. Well, I tell you, we just had a,

speaker: Speaker 2
words: we just go right back and did it again. See, we didn't have to pay cash for groceries, just like in the city you have to pay cash for your groceries. We didn't have to, maybe we were able to run up to two or three hundred dollars for groceries. Of course, there was a house rent to be paid. Sometimes that was lying back too, until he got back to work. But he was all, you know, he's, that's why he would borrow money to pay that off, see. Then we'd have to pay that off.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, that interest then, you'd have to pay.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So that was, that was the way it was at that time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So it really wasn't very secure at all.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, we got a lot better situation now than I did.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I was going to show you something here that you never seen before. All right. That's one wool and three pieces. Oh, so it is. Yes, yes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Quite a rigging job.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It certainly is. Oh, look at that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's where he just wrapped it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: See that? See how they're even split? Yeah. That sure is. Is that what that tool does? Uh-huh. Yeah, they rig it. That's what it's called. Did you make that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I did. Yeah, years ago.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I made it with a couple of old pitchfork handles. Oh, I didn't know about that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You made that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, I worked for farmer one time. He wouldn't pay me, so I cut the orc.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Don't believe him.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He's got a hearing with him.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He's kidding you. He's kidding you.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, I got him. That's a good trick there. See, that's what, then I smoothed it down with a knife. And then I'd use the rapid. Uh-huh. Like that. Uh-huh. Well, let's see. I asked you, you aren't much involved in church.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, not really. I go to church. If I wait for him, he's in full progress. But when I want to go by myself, I go. And I like to get in. I like to have, I like to do the things I want to do, you know. And I like to, he likes baking cakes or something, or the outside.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Before that, that was my job. Oh, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That really was nice.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I didn't realize before that willows came in such different colors.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Aren't they beautiful? Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yeah, but like, right now, those, who was good, this kind. Uh-huh. Of course, it's good, but there's others. Even around the light part of September, they're good again. Then you get the old kind of colors. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. I want to thank you for taking me off of it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But right now, that's all you're going to get, the same kind. And that was not very long either, because the sap run, and you get too much sap, and then it breaks. Then it breaks, and then it's tender, you know. Then I have to buy the whole year. So it's only seasonal, which you can collect the... You know, my teacher told me, you know, the monsoon that, who was good, he said, remember that. January, February, March, April, May, quit. May quit. Why? Because the sap up. All up. It's much hard. Uh-huh. All the monsoon, it's got a hard in it, good for, to make a wool, to use the wool. Start the, uh, September. May, that's in some years, this year was good, it was cold, better, you know. It stayed cold longer. But another way, you can use it, right. This year, then, I generally get the summer ahead, you know. Now, we got to go to, uh, Pugamon, next, uh, what, next Friday?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: The 14th, 13th.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Next Friday.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: 13th, no, week from Friday.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So, I got to show them how to, to make a, how I make a basket, you know. And they ask me to come, they say, come and buy people with me. They'll try this thing for me, you know, I need it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I might, I might just take it off.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: All the time, you see, the old men, we shouldn't keep them, don't order some basket, you know. I have some, they show them, you know. And then it's, order, I tell them, I didn't order. She's supposed to take the orders, but she's gone, I don't care.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She's been working inside, I was inside. Aren't we tiny. What are you going to do with my tiny? What am I going to do with my tiny?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, they're fortunate to have found someone like you. And then, I mean, we would go to the expo, for a week. I would make a lot of basket for them. Make it a giveaway.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's one of the nicest things that happened to us.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You couldn't sell it, but you could take the order, you take a quarter of the order. And I was pretty pleased with it. Are you filling orders now? Is that what you're making out there? Whoop, whoop.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You fall down. You fall down, oh now you're mad. I'll be taking a push now. Okay.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, you get, you take a few baskets, that's what you do. I think it's very interesting. Oh, I know, they sell like hotcakes. Yes. Oh, yes. Some ladies, couple ladies, they got a business there in Moscow. I mean, a cool one. They buy baskets from me a lot of times. I think that's the old mold shop, is this?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Is that one? I don't know what it is. There's one shop there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, they buy a hundred dollars worth.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know what, what's the name of it?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, and then they sell them for $300. Then they're business, they're selling, you know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I just assume you get, sell to my friends, you know, because one day I said that, I asked them, what did you charge for so and so, and she said, well, I don't know, but it was a lot more than what she gave.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, yeah. Oh, they make plenty in their town. So it's better if you can just, yeah, I do it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because when my friends come to me, I just assume, sell to them, you know. We've had lots of, Moscow, lots from Moscow. And they got me kind of spoiled when they, on Saturday and Sunday, I expect some Moscow, Pullman, you know. And I'm so tickled when somebody comes, especially weekends, because it's kind of lonely. And the last Sunday now, Dale from, brought, I think, four people in from, from Pullman. And I really enjoyed that, too. I just gave you up, I looked pretty up to you, but I was hoping you'd come to Dainesville. I'd come every week if I could, because my car's broke down.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think it's kind of nice to have something to draw people to your house.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think it's nice to think that, that the younger generation likes to come to the older generation, you know. That's the, that's the grand feeling. Because, I always said, when you get old, well, you just push to one side and nobody cares, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It happens to a lot of people.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, it does. And you feel, I feel like I, I, I'd like to be needed, you know. And I don't care what it is. I'd like, I've had a lot of people tell me, well, you just don't have time to do the things that you wanted to do. And I said, well, I don't expect anybody to do things for me, but I'd like to be known that I'm needed. And I'd drop anything to do something for somebody else, because it's, because I want to, you know. A lot of times I do sewing and stuff, and I'm getting suffered. Well, I just, I just turn it down with, and go ahead and finish with the sewing, and they can come and get it, and I, my stuff gets done anyway, and I'll have that job done too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay, let's see. If you knew a young woman who was starting out in the kind of life you've had, what do you think she'd need to know?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What should she need to know? The things that I went through? Uh-huh. Oh, I don't know. I just, I would feel sorry for one thing. And, uh, I just, well, I don't know. I don't know how to explain it myself, because I'd hate to have anybody else go through this life I had to live. You know, sometimes I wish the things I did go through, I wish I wrote all of it down in shorthand. I wouldn't believe it myself. You could have written a book. Uh-huh. I wouldn't want anybody to live like I had to live. I want somebody to live better than I do, than I had to live.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But you've learned to cope with a lot of problems. But I've learned to cope with a lot of it. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Even since we've been married, there's been hard times. It's not been goody, goody, goody. But, uh, I have it better today than I did 20 years ago, because I have a home, and, of course, 20 years ago I had a home too, but maybe it wasn't as nice as it is today, but I feel more secure now too, for some reason or another. Maybe it's because the children are all married and got their own families,

speaker: Speaker 1
words: and I know they're taken care of.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Someone else takes care of them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And they aren't dependent on you. Uh-huh. And they're here close, but they kind of look out for you a little bit. Right. Right. There's a certain comfort in knowing them.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's right.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you have, do you take magazines or newspapers? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, once in a while, I have had the Lewiston paper, but my subscription ran out, and my gracious, I... Forty-eight fifty a year is kind of, is an awful lot to put out when you're just getting on your little social security, so I haven't... This paper here, somebody else was giving it to us, an Anderson. So, I haven't got any papers for quite a while, ourself, but it doesn't, when he doesn't give us a paper anymore, I think I will get it for John, because he kind of enjoys it. And I do too. You've got to have a little bit of something from other works, from other parts of the world, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you watch, do you have TV?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, we watch TV. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What favorite shows?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What favorite, well, I'll tell you, my really favorite one is As the World Turns. And the news, I do like the news. And, um, I like sewing, I like Rota. And, um, all that... I'm right offhand, I can't tell you, but a lot of news, ones I do like. I like all quiz shows, anything that's real.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: More than the fiction type.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I don't care too much. I might watch, but I'm not crazy about it, I can leave it, you know, but I do like all the real stuff. The good.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you and your husband share on making decisions, talk about things, or were there certain things he...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I hate to tell you this, but it's not true. We don't. If it's, I ask him now, what would you like for supper tonight? Well, anything you fix is fine. So and so is coming up, what should I do? Whatever you decide is fine. He never wants to think, so I'm really more or less on my own.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He wants you to make the decision.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He wants me to make the decision. I don't know whether he can't make the decision, or whether he thinks that his decision isn't the right thing for me to believe. I don't know what his idea is, but we've never... And I just love to talk something over with him. Well, you know best what to do. You do what you think is right.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Has it always been like that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Always been that way. So I just more or less be on my own. I do all the... I would get the checks, he signs it, I sign mine, and go to the bank, and I make up all the bills, and we have to have stuff for different things. I'm the one that has to do it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's quite a contrast from your father, then.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes. My daddy was very different. My mother never had... My mother didn't have a darned name, I don't think, until after my folks were divorced, finally. Well, this is an awful thing to say. They're both dead now. But I often wish that my mother and dad had divorced when we were all home. I really do. I really did wish that, desperately, because my mother, I always used to say to my mom, Mom, how come you live with Daddy when he does all this? You know it's not right. And she'd go, well, how would I support you children? I'd say, you know what, Mother, I think you would be a lot better off in a lot of ways, just knowing that I couldn't support the kids. She didn't have an education, you know. Kids just like me, she worked in the time she could walk around. But my mother lived with us until we were all married, and she just divorced me.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How did she make a living for herself then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, he had to support her, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: By law, she was required to pay all the loans.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She found out more things after she got divorced. If she'd have got divorced and we were home, she'd have had a lot better, because he would have had to support us too. But this way, you only supported her. But she married twice afterwards, and she was happy in each one. And I hate to say this, but I had a lot better stepdad than I had my own dad. And that's a terrible, terrible, terrible... God forgive me, because that's the truth. It's an awful thing to say. I'd hate to have my kids say that, but... But they can't, because he's been... he's a really good daddy, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That old German, that terrible system kind of... Yeah. Because your husband has a German background.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, yeah, well, it's the opposite. There is a difference. There is a difference, yeah. Very kind-hearted and very soft-hearted.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was your father Northern German, Prussian?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't... I really don't know. I didn't know he was just a hard, hard man. And it didn't bother me. You do what I tell you, or else the strap is right there, and you got it. I was 17 years old, the last thing I ever got, and that's when I walked out. And I don't know, this is something that's been striking. And I was in... I don't know to this day where I was. He would never tell me. It just seemed like he had to have someone to beat on all the time. And it's just something, you know, some of those German people, that... they're just harsh, that's all I can say.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Some of them.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Some of them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I asked you about the Depression, but I don't think I've asked you about what the war years were like here in Elk River.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: War years?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: World War II.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well... That was real. I wasn't married then. 1942? Oh, that one! Oh, yeah. That's the other one, I think. Oh, um... Well, I don't know. 1942, that wasn't too bad, I don't think.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Let's see.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That was me, no, I was just two years old. I was young, it was working, as far as I know. So I think it was a dire match. In fact, I think, wasn't the job pretty good at that time? Wasn't the wages good at that time?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think that was true.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think the wages were...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Except I understand that some of the young men were away from the community.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. Well, see, my husband was...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The times were better then.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. I don't think we had any trouble at all at that time. There was a lot more money then, for some reason or another, than there was before, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Mm-hmm. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, it was a time of prosperity, as far as factories and things were. Yeah. And, you see, I've never lived in a big city, so I don't know nothing about the big city. So actually you weren't very much aware of the big city. No, I don't know nothing about the bed line or none of that stuff.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That was with the Depression.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, that was with the Depression, yeah. But I mean, that was all in the bigger cities.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We're here, there's always more left.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Mrs. Morris has lived here for a long time. Have you known her all this time?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, yeah, they were here when we... See, I knew her husband. He was a grand person, wonderful person. Yes, they were here before... I guess they were one of the first ones that came here, from what I understood.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: She talked about having groups of women that worked on making bandages and knitting

speaker: Speaker 2
words: and things like that. Oh, no, I didn't... I don't...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You weren't in on that? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because I don't believe in that stuff.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You had a young child.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I guess she did do a lot of that stuff. But I was never in on any of that stuff.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So some older women maybe.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, it must have been that kind of thing. The church women that did some of that stuff, too. I never did go into a function or any of that stuff.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I've asked you an awful lot about your life.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I've talked my blues.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you have anything else you'd like to add to it?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I don't know if anything else. I was like, I've got to think of what to say. I've enjoyed both of you so much. And your name's what?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Isabel Miller.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And this here is... Julia. Julia. I should all remember, because I got such a Julie.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, Julia.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, Julia was the name. Okay. Julia, yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The reason why you've always stayed in Elk River was mostly his work. Yeah. That's what decided you.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, right. Because he had a job here. But now the last three years he wants to get out. But the next question is trying to sell our house. We would like to sell our house. And then the next question is could you get enough out of it to go somewhere to buy another house or rent. It's so viciously high that...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You might be better off if you bought a trailer.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, that's what I know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I love that. They're a lot cheaper than houses and maybe it could be a lot better for you.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I would like to have a trailer. I'd have one put in Detroit where my daughter lives, but she lives on the side hill too. I would love to live on a flat once. She would love to live on a flat. Although I love this home up here, but I'd give it up for a fair price and say, well, I'm moving tomorrow, ha-ha, I've sold my house. But it don't go that way.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You'd solve the problems that came with that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I could tell them, if this house is sold tomorrow, I would take me all night, and it wouldn't take me long to get there. I'd have a sale, a yard sale. It wouldn't be very much I'd take with me.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Wouldn't you miss all these friends you've made around here that pop in on you? You'd make new friends.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'd make new friends.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You'd have more people popping in on you if you were closer to Moscow.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's what I was going to say. If I moved back to Detroit or to Moscow or even out of Moscow or Pullman, I know good and well I'd have a lot more company than I would here, because I'd say, how come you don't come up? I miss you. How come you don't? You live so far away. Well, I live just as far from you as you do from me. I don't live any farther from you. But they can't get that through their mind that it's just as far from me to live. Where I live, it's from where you live. They go where they live. So I would really like to. We've been trying to sell our house, but, well, I just haven't had too much of a – maybe I go the wrong way. Someone said if I put it in a real estate, but then they take a big chunk out of it, too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I put it in just Moscow paper.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: A lot of people do that. Oh, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think sometimes the most choices go people sell for themselves. The problem places they can't sell, they list with a real estate dealer.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, you think so?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's been the experience I've seen.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You mean like you put it in a real estate, it's the one you can't sell?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Right, right. We've had lots of offers. It's the lottery first that – Yeah, the people who place with the realtor are usually the ones who are moving right away and can't be around to sell their house. So they use the realtor to sell. Or it's a place that's a real problem. There might be something wrong with the place, or they maybe want too much for it, and things like that. But you might try just advertising.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I wouldn't mind just putting the paper. It wouldn't cost much to put the paper.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: A few dollars, I figure.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And then that's another situation. I'd have to do it all by myself because my husband wouldn't know. First thing about it, I'd have to go to somebody that knew something about it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think your daughter could help write up the ad. Yeah. And you would have to – you could probably get a real estate dealer or a lawyer to help. I've got the contract.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think I would go to a lawyer. I think. Or either some place that somebody would know enough about it. You'd want it to happen legally. Yeah, because I don't want no loopholes. And so I would – they say you should – well, they told me, why don't you put in California paper because they're the ones that want to come out to Idaho. I said, well, I don't know. That's kind of far-fetched. I said, well, I don't know if I want to do that or not. So I don't know. I said, listen, California.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I said, well, you can pass the word around if you want to.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But I'd like to lean on somebody once in a while. You know, I need someone to lean on. But like I said hundreds of times, I've got a husband. I sure need a man, you know, to lean on my – to lean on my – have him to tell me what to do or am I doing the right thing or –

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You'd like to be able to talk it over with him. Right.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Get some other viewpoint. And he doesn't understand anything. Of course, he's got his troops, so I understand. All he's got in his mind is his basket and I'd like to come in here, you know. He doesn't understand what we're talking about. He doesn't know nothing at all. All he's got in his mind is my basket.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He's got it back in his childhood.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So you are so right. I said, what are you going to have for supper tonight? And I know what I think about. I've got to make the lid for that basket now. I said, I asked you what you want for supper. What do you want to fix? Well, I'm just – well, I wasn't aware of it when I first started in the beginning.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Does he always eat what you fix?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah. He's very easy. Very easy. I can fix him a – Now, most people say they don't want no – they don't want any sandwich for dinner or anything. He always says, make me a sandwich. Make me a sandwich. Even for supper sometimes, make me a sandwich. I'm hungry.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I said, well, I'm going to get supper. Oh, that's all right.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He just always wants something to eat. He don't care. He's very easy to cook with for, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I've got to – I promised Julie I'd get her back the second time.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, and late. I don't know what time it is. Oh. Let's see.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think it's in –

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I signed – that was the only one I did.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you want to check the second one then? You don't care how we use it? No, I don't care what you do.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Okay. It's just fine. I blabbered my mouth off and I –

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You didn't tell anything you didn't care about?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. All right. Here's your signature right here and down here. And then I'll sign it and give you half of it then.
